domainCoverage.synopsis: High-throughput vector search, low-latency embedding retrieval, and resilient model inference pipelines under dynamic token generation workloads.

chapters.title: Vector Embeddings & Similarity
chapters.summary: Vector embeddings map text, images, or code into dense fixed-length coordinate spaces where semantic proximity translates to geometric closeness, measured via cosine similarity, dot product, or Euclidean distance.

chapters.title: Embedding Model Selection
chapters.summary: Embedding models map text, code, or multimodal inputs into dense (or sparse) vectors where geometric distance captures semantic similarity for RAG, search, and clustering.

chapters.title: Vector Databases & RAG
chapters.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) grounds LLM outputs by indexing domain documents as dense/sparse vectors and retrieving top-k relevant chunks at query time via approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) indexes like HNSW.

chapters.title: HNSW Vector Indexing & Approximate Nearest Neighbors
chapters.summary: HNSW organizes high-dimensional vectors into a hierarchy of proximity graphs—sparse long-range highways on top and a dense base graph on Layer 0—delivering O(log N) search at >98% recall.

chapters.title: Hybrid Vector Search (BM25 + HNSW + RRF)
chapters.summary: Hybrid vector search combines sparse lexical scoring (BM25) with dense semantic embeddings (HNSW/IVF) via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) and optional cross-encoder reranking to achieve high recall on both exact identifiers and conceptual queries.

chapters.title: RAG Retrieval Pipelines
chapters.summary: Production RAG retrieval combines semantic chunking, hybrid dense (HNSW) + sparse (BM25/SPLADE) search, Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), metadata pre-filtering, and cross-encoder reranking to deliver high-precision context to LLMs.

chapters.title: Context Compression for RAG
chapters.summary: Techniques that prune, rerank, or summarize retrieved RAG chunks before LLM generation to slash token cost and TTFT while beating 'lost-in-the-middle' attention decay.

chapters.title: Deep Learning Foundations: Backpropagation, Transformers & Optimizers
chapters.summary: Modern deep learning combines reverse-mode automatic differentiation (backpropagation), parallelizable sequence modeling via scaled dot-product self-attention (Transformers), and adaptive momentum-based gradient updates (AdamW) to train multi-billion-parameter networks stably.

chapters.title: Transformer Attention
chapters.summary: Self-attention lets every token dynamically weight and aggregate information from all other tokens in a sequence in parallel, replacing sequential recurrent bottlenecks with matrix multiplications over Query, Key, and Value projections.

chapters.title: Model Serving & GPU Batching
chapters.summary: Group concurrent inference requests into tensor batches on the GPU to shift workloads from memory-bandwidth-bound to compute-bound without blowing tail latency.

chapters.title: LLM Quantization, GPTQ/AWQ & Inference Performance
chapters.summary: LLM quantization compresses 16-bit model weights and KV caches into 8-bit or 4-bit representations (FP8, AWQ, GPTQ, GGUF) to slash VRAM usage by 2-4x and accelerate memory-bandwidth-bound token generation.

chapters.title: Semantic Caching for LLMs
chapters.summary: Semantic LLM caching intercepts natural-language prompts, embeds them into dense vectors (e.g., 1536-dim via text-embedding-3-small), and performs an Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) lookup in a vector store like Redis or Qdrant. When cosine similarity clears a strict threshold (typically 0.93–0.96), the system returns a cached completion in 20–45 ms instead of paying 1.5–6 seconds and $0.01–$0.05 per frontier model inference.

chapters.title: LLM Fine-Tuning & LoRA
chapters.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes a pretrained LLM's weights and trains tiny rank-decomposed adapter matrices, cutting fine-tuning VRAM by 3–10x while preserving base capabilities.

chapters.title: LLM Agent Tool Use
chapters.summary: LLM Agent Tool Use pairs a language model with typed JSON Schema function definitions and a runtime loop (e.g., ReAct), enabling the model to emit structured tool calls, execute deterministic code or APIs, and condition its next reasoning step on grounded observations.

chapters.title: Prompt Injection Defenses
chapters.summary: Prompt injection defense prevents untrusted user inputs or retrieved external content (RAG chunks, emails, web pages) from hijacking an LLM's control plane and triggering unauthorized tool calls or data exfiltration.

chapters.title: Prompt Engineering, LLM Reasoning & Thinking Models
chapters.summary: Systematic design of system instructions, context layout, delimiters, and constrained output schemas to make LLM behavior reliable, cache-friendly, and production-grade.

chapters.title: Multi-Agent Orchestration
chapters.summary: Multi-agent orchestration coordinates specialized LLM agents—each with scoped prompts, tools, and memory—using explicit control topologies like supervisor graphs, handoff swarms, or DAG pipelines.

chapters.title: AI Agents, LangGraph & Stateful Tool Orchestration
chapters.summary: Stateful LLM agents model multi-step reasoning, tool calls, and human approvals as explicit directed cyclic graphs rather than fragile, unbounded while-loops.

chapters.title: LLM Evaluation Harnesses
chapters.summary: An automated testing and scoring pipeline that measures LLM accuracy, safety, latency, and cost across curated datasets before and after every prompt, model, or retrieval change.

chapters.title: ML Feature Stores (Online & Offline)
chapters.summary: A feature store is a dual-plane ML data platform that computes, versions, and serves consistent features across both batch model training (offline) and low-latency real-time inference (online).

chapters.title: ML Pipeline Orchestration
chapters.summary: Coordinate multi-stage data prep, distributed training, evaluation, and deployment as idempotent, lineage-tracked DAGs rather than fragile cron scripts.

domainDeepDive.whyItMatters: Integrating modern Large Language Models (LLMs) and vector embeddings into production software presents unprecedented engineering challenges: unbounded generation latencies (seconds vs milliseconds), token streaming backpressure, massive GPU memory footprints, and non-deterministic statistical outputs. Modern engineers must treat ML not as magical black boxes, but as high-latency, memory-constrained distributed I/O systems requiring rigorous caching, semantic validation, and fault-tolerant fallbacks.
domainDeepDive.keyTakeaway: Treat AI model inference as a high-latency, token-streaming distributed I/O workload. Optimize vector search geometries, cache intermediate embeddings aggressively, decouple model latency with asynchronous queues, and enforce semantic guardrails.
coreArchitectureRules: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) Recall vs Latency: Exact cosine similarity search over millions of high-dimensional vectors (D >= 1536) is computationally prohibitive (O(N * D)). HNSW and IVF graph indexes trade minute recall precision (98%) for sub-10ms search latencies.

KV-Cache Memory Invariant & Dynamic Batching: Autoregressive transformer models require storing Key-Value tensor projections for every generated token. PagedAttention and continuous dynamic batching maximize GPU Tensor Core utilization and prevent out-of-memory crashes.

Hybrid Search & Reciprocal Rank Fusion: Dense vector search captures semantic concepts but misses exact keyword matches (IDs, error codes). Hybrid retrieval combining dense embeddings with sparse BM25 lexical search provides superior retrieval accuracy.

Streaming Backpressure & Client Disconnect Lifecycle: Large LLM responses emit tokens over Server-Sent Events (SSE) for 10-30 seconds. Systems must detect client disconnects immediately to cancel active GPU generation and prevent wasted compute.

Deterministic Semantic Guardrails & Evals: Never deploy probabilistic LLM outputs directly to critical APIs without automated schema validation (JSON schema validation, Pydantic) and adversarial prompt-injection guardrails.

learningJourney.title: Vector Embeddings, Mathematical Spaces & Similarity
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how unstructured data maps to continuous vector spaces and how distance metrics behave on hardware.

explanation.foundation: Embedding models project text, images, or code into dense floating-point vectors in R^D (commonly D = 768 to 3072).
explanation.core: Choosing between Cosine similarity, Euclidean (L2) distance, and Inner Product depends on whether vector magnitude carries signal. When vectors are L2-normalized to unit length (||v|| = 1), Euclidean squared distance reduces to 2 - 2(a · b), making Cosine, L2, and Dot Product rank-equivalent while letting CPUs compute similarity as raw AVX-512 or NEON SIMD dot products.
explanation.deepDive: In high dimensions, random vector distances concentrate around their mean (curse of dimensionality), so models trained with contrastive or Matryoshka losses are required to preserve meaningful angular separation.

benefits: Invariant to vector magnitude; focuses purely on semantic direction.
Reduces to a single dot product when embeddings are pre-normalized at ingest.
costs: Ignores document length or popularity signals if magnitude encodes importance.
Requires extra norm division at query time if vectors are not pre-normalized.

benefits: Preserves both magnitude and directional separation.
Natural fit for spatial clustering (k-means) and anomaly detection.
costs: Sensitive to unnormalized scale differences across heterogeneous encoders.
Higher arithmetic cost per comparison (subtractions + squaring) than raw dot product.

benefits: Fastest hardware execution via fused multiply-add (FMA) SIMD instructions.
Allows embedding models to encode prior popularity or confidence in vector norm.
costs: Unbounded score range complicates threshold-based semantic caching.
High-norm outlier vectors can dominate top-k results unfairly.

ideas.title: Unit Normalization at Ingest
ideas.description: Normalize embeddings to unit L2 norm once during ingestion so query-time cosine similarity executes as a pure SIMD dot product without square-root or division instructions.

ideas.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)
ideas.description: Models trained with MRL pack coarse semantics into early dimensions, allowing a 3072-d vector to be truncated to 512-d or 256-d for fast first-stage retrieval before full-dimension rescoring.

example.title: Pre-normalizing 1536-d embeddings for AVX-512 throughput
example.scenario: A semantic product-matching service ran cosine similarity across 200,000 candidate vectors per shard and hit CPU saturation during peak traffic.
example.reasoning: Profiling showed 32% of query CPU cycles went to computing vector norms on the fly. Pre-normalizing vectors at write time and switching the index metric to inner product enabled contiguous AVX-512 FMA dot products, cutting p95 scoring CPU time by 35% with identical top-k rankings.
example.lesson: Pre-normalize unit vectors at ingestion so query-time similarity becomes pure SIMD multiply-add.

learningJourney.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) & Vector Indexing
learningJourney.purpose: Trade bounded recall loss for sub-10ms latency and predictable RAM budgets at million-to-billion vector scale.

explanation.foundation: Exact K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) scans every vector in O(N * D) time, saturating DRAM bandwidth long before compute.
explanation.core: Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes eliminate exhaustive scans. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph where upper sparse layers act as express highways and lower dense layers refine the local neighborhood in O(log N) hops, tuned via M (edges per node), efConstruction, and efSearch.
explanation.deepDive: Inverted File (IVF) indexes partition the space into k Voronoi cells via k-means and scan only the nearest nprobe cells. To fit billion-scale corpora in RAM, Product Quantization (PQ) splits a D-dimensional vector into M sub-vectors and encodes each to an 8-bit centroid ID—compressing a 1536-d FP32 vector (6,144 bytes) down to 96 bytes (64x compression) at the cost of slight quantization error.

benefits: High recall (97-99%) at sub-10ms p99 latency without centroid training.
Supports incremental inserts and deletes with strong query-time QPS.
costs: High RAM overhead (raw vectors plus graph adjacency lists).
Slow index build times and expensive in-memory tombstones on heavy deletes.

benefits: 10x-64x smaller memory footprint via sub-vector centroid codebooks.
Predictable linear scan over nprobe cells with high cache locality.
costs: Requires periodic k-means/codebook retraining as data distribution drifts.
Lower recall unless paired with a second-stage disk/RAM rescore of top candidates.

ideas.title: Two-Stage Oversampling and Rescoring
ideas.description: Retrieve top 4*K candidates using compressed int8 or PQ codes in RAM, then fetch full-precision FP32/FP16 vectors from NVMe or RAM to compute exact distances for the final top K.

ideas.title: Segment-Based Immutable Indexing
ideas.description: Buffer live vector writes in a WAL and small mutable segment while merging immutable HNSW segments asynchronously in the background so compaction never stalls query threads.

example.title: Fitting 50M 1536-d vectors into a 64 GB RAM node
example.scenario: Storing 50M 1536-d FP32 vectors in an unquantized HNSW graph required ~360 GB of RAM, forcing an expensive 6-node memory-optimized cluster.
example.reasoning: Switched to Scalar Quantization (int8) with HNSW oversampling (4x) and exact FP16 rescoring from NVMe. RAM dropped by 74% to ~52 GB on a single node while keeping recall@10 at 98.1% and p99 latency at 11ms.
example.lesson: Quantize in-memory index vectors and oversample + rescore exact vectors from fast storage.

reflectionQuestions: What is the total RAM footprint of raw vectors plus HNSW graph edges (M * 2 * 4 bytes/node) at your 12-month target scale?
How does selectivity of metadata filters affect HNSW graph connectivity during pre-filtering vs. post-filtering?
What recall@K degradation is acceptable in exchange for 4x-16x quantization compression?
How will your index handle high update/delete churn without accumulating HNSW tombstone bloat?

learningJourney.title: Hybrid Search: Dense Semantic Vectors & Sparse BM25
learningJourney.purpose: Combine conceptual semantic recall with exact lexical precision using calibrated rank fusion.

explanation.foundation: Dense bi-encoder embeddings compress entire passages into a single fixed-width vector, which blurs rare tokens, exact SKUs, stack traces, and invoice IDs.
explanation.core: Sparse lexical algorithms like BM25 score exact term matches using saturated term frequency (k1) and document-length normalization (b) weighted by Inverse Document Frequency (IDF), while neural sparse models like SPLADE expand documents into learned vocabulary weights. Because BM25 scores are unbounded positive floats and cosine scores lie in [-1, 1], summing raw scores directly is unstable.
explanation.deepDive: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists purely by position: RRF(d) = sum(1 / (k + rank_i(d))) with k = 60, ensuring documents ranked highly by both retrievers rise deterministically.

ideas.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
ideas.description: Fuse dense and sparse rankings using 1 / (60 + rank) so neither retriever's raw score scale dominates without fragile min-max calibration.

ideas.title: SPLADE Learned Sparse Expansion
ideas.description: Use a masked-language-model head to project passages into high-dimensional sparse vectors that capture synonyms (e.g. 'car' -> 'automobile') while remaining compatible with inverted indexes.

example.title: Sub-20ms hybrid semantic search at 10M document scale
example.scenario: An enterprise document platform using pure dense embeddings failed when finance teams searched exact invoice IDs like 'INV-90210' or error codes like 'ERR_QUOTA_429', returning topically similar but wrong memos.
example.reasoning: Deployed parallel Qdrant HNSW dense retrieval and BM25 inverted-index search, merging top-100 candidates from each leg via RRF (k = 60). Exact identifier recall hit 99.4% and overall NDCG@10 improved by 42% at 18ms p95 latency.
example.lesson: Pair dense embeddings with sparse lexical retrieval via RRF whenever queries include exact identifiers or domain jargon.

reflectionQuestions: Which query classes in your workload require exact token matching (IDs, error codes, proper nouns) vs. semantic paraphrasing?
Should dense and sparse legs carry equal weight in RRF, or do domain benchmarks justify weighted rank fusion?
How do you tokenize compound technical identifiers (camelCase, snake_case, hyphenated SKUs) in your BM25 analyzer?
What is the tail-latency impact of running dense and sparse queries in parallel and waiting for the slower leg?

learningJourney.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Architecture
learningJourney.purpose: Design multi-stage retrieval pipelines that ground LLM generation in fresh, access-controlled data.

explanation.foundation: Naive RAG—embed a raw user query, fetch top-k chunks, and stuff them into a prompt—fails on ambiguous phrasing, multi-hop questions, and strict ACL filtering.
explanation.core: Short user questions occupy a different region of embedding space than long declarative answers; HyDE bridges this gap by generating a hypothetical answer first and embedding that passage. Multi-query expansion and sub-query decomposition split compound requests into parallel retrievals.
explanation.deepDive: Equally critical is enforcing tenant and document permissions via metadata pre-filtering inside the index rather than post-filtering, which can return zero results when an authorized subset is small.

example.reasoning: Added an LLM query decomposer that split the prompt into two parallel sub-queries scoped by quarter metadata filters ('Q1 policy' and 'Q2 EMEA churn'), then merged results before synthesis. Answer faithfulness on the eval suite rose from 61% to 93%.

learningJourney.title: Chunking Strategies, Context Compression & Reranking
learningJourney.purpose: Maximize signal-to-noise ratio in the LLM context window through smart chunking and cross-encoder reranking.

explanation.foundation: Bi-encoder embeddings encode queries and documents independently in O(1) vector lookups, losing fine-grained token-to-token interactions.
explanation.core: Cross-encoders concatenate (query, chunk) and run full self-attention across both, producing dramatically more accurate relevance scores at O((L_q + L_d)^2) compute cost—making them ideal as a second-stage filter over the top 50–100 hybrid hits. Chunking faces a core tension: small chunks (128–256 tokens) yield sharp embeddings, while LLMs need surrounding context (1024+ tokens) to reason accurately.
explanation.deepDive: Parent-child indexing resolves this by indexing small child chunks while returning their parent section to the generator, and placing the highest-ranked chunks at the start and end of the prompt mitigates the 'Lost in the Middle' attention decay.

caveats: Cross-encoder latency scales linearly with candidate count K; cap reranking to top 30-50 chunks or run on dedicated GPU batching.
Fixed-character chunking splits tables, code blocks, and sentences mid-thought; use structure-aware or recursive splitters.
Stuffing 30+ chunks into long-context windows inflates TTFT (Time to First Token) quadratically during prefill and degrades accuracy.

ideas.title: Parent-Child Retrieval
ideas.description: Embed 150-token child windows for high retrieval precision, then map hits back to their 1,000-token parent block for coherent LLM synthesis.

ideas.title: Edge-Weighted Context Ordering
ideas.description: Place the top-1 and top-2 reranked passages at the beginning and end of the prompt context to counter U-shaped transformer attention decay.

example.title: Eliminating missed clauses in 100-page legal contract QA
example.scenario: A legal assistant injected top-30 500-token chunks into the prompt, yet the LLM repeatedly missed exception clauses placed in chunks 12 through 22.
example.reasoning: Switched to clause-aware parent-child indexing (200-token child chunks linked to full section parents) and added a BGE-reranker-v2 cross-encoder to prune top-50 hits down to the top 5 ordered at prompt edges. Hallucinated or missed exceptions dropped by 68% and prefill latency fell 45%.
example.lesson: Rerank aggressively to a small, high-signal context rather than relying on raw context-window size.

reflectionQuestions: What document structures (markdown headers, tables, code ASTs) should govern your chunk boundaries?
Is a 40-80ms cross-encoder rerank step justified by the resulting drop in downstream LLM token cost and hallucinations?
How do you deduplicate overlapping parent blocks when multiple child chunks match the same section?
Have you evaluated whether placing critical context at the prompt edges changes answer accuracy?

learningJourney.title: Deep Learning Foundations & GPU Tensor Hardware
learningJourney.purpose: Understand tensor memory layouts, autograd graphs, Tensor Cores, and the GPU Roofline model.

explanation.foundation: Deep learning workloads are governed by GPU hardware physics.
explanation.core: Tensors are N-dimensional views over contiguous 1D memory buffers indexed via shape and stride metadata; non-contiguous transposes must be materialized before coalesced GPU memory reads. Training builds a dynamic or static computation graph for reverse-mode automatic differentiation (autograd), storing intermediate activations in VRAM unless activation checkpointing recomputes them on the fly.
explanation.deepDive: On modern GPUs, Tensor Cores execute warp-level Matrix Multiply-Accumulate (MMA) in FP16, BF16, or FP8 at hundreds of teraflops. By the Roofline model, arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved from HBM) determines whether an operation is compute-bound (LLM prompt prefill, large GEMMs) or memory-bandwidth-bound (token-by-token LLM decode, elementwise activations).

ideas.title: Prefill vs. Decode Roofline Split
ideas.description: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel as large matrix-matrix multiplications (compute-bound), whereas autoregressive decode processes 1 token per sequence per step (HBM bandwidth-bound).

ideas.title: BF16 & FP8 Precision Trade-offs
ideas.description: BF16 preserves FP32's 8-bit exponent range to prevent training gradient underflow, while FP8 cuts weight and KV-cache HBM traffic in half during inference.

example.title: Breaking the HBM bandwidth wall in 70B decode
example.scenario: A 70B FP16 model on 2x H100 GPUs showed only 8% Tensor Core compute utilization during decode despite 100% HBM bandwidth saturation.
example.reasoning: Each decode step streamed ~140 GB of weights from HBM for a single token per request. Quantizing weights to FP8 (halving HBM bytes per token) and enabling continuous batching raised arithmetic intensity across concurrent sequences, boosting decode tokens/sec by 2.4x.
example.lesson: Autoregressive LLM decode is gated by HBM memory bandwidth; increase batching or quantize weights to raise arithmetic intensity.

reflectionQuestions: Which phase of your inference pipeline is compute-bound (TTFT/prefill) vs. HBM bandwidth-bound (ITL/decode)?
When does kernel fusion (e.g., `torch.compile` / Triton) eliminate intermediate HBM round-trips for elementwise ops?
How much VRAM must be reserved for activation memory vs. model weights vs. KV-cache?
Does FP8 or INT4 AWQ quantization introduce unacceptable perplexity or tool-calling regression on your eval set?

learningJourney.title: Transformer Architecture & Attention Physics
learningJourney.purpose: Master attention math, FlashAttention SRAM tiling, GQA/MQA, RoPE, and PagedAttention KV-caching.

explanation.foundation: Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where scaling by sqrt(d_k) keeps dot-product variance near 1 so softmax gradients do not vanish.
explanation.core: Materializing the N x N attention matrix in HBM scales quadratically in memory and bandwidth; FlashAttention tiles Q, K, and V blocks into fast on-chip GPU SRAM and computes softmax incrementally via online rescaling, keeping memory O(N). During autoregressive generation, caching past K and V tensors avoids recomputing the prefix, but KV-cache size (2 * layers * kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_param * seq_len) quickly dominates VRAM.
explanation.deepDive: Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares K/V heads across groups of Q heads to shrink KV-cache traffic, RoPE encodes relative token positions via 2D rotations, and PagedAttention allocates KV-cache in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks to eliminate fragmentation.

ideas.title: FlashAttention Online Softmax Tiling
ideas.description: Fuse QK^T, masking, softmax, and V multiplication inside GPU SRAM tiles so the quadratic N x N score matrix is never written to slow HBM.

ideas.title: PagedAttention Virtual KV Blocks
ideas.description: Manage KV-cache like OS virtual memory pages so sequences grow dynamically without reserving contiguous max-context VRAM buffers.

example.title: Eliminating 60% VRAM waste with PagedAttention and continuous batching
example.scenario: A customer-support AI cluster on 8x A100 GPUs suffered OOM crashes during morning traffic spikes and dropped 14% of active sessions due to static max-length KV-cache pre-allocation.
example.reasoning: Migrated serving to vLLM using PagedAttention and iteration-level continuous batching. KV-cache internal fragmentation dropped from ~60% to under 4%, quadrupling concurrent request capacity and cutting monthly GPU spend by 58%.
example.lesson: KV-cache memory management—not raw FLOPs—determines concurrent LLM serving capacity.

reflectionQuestions: What is the exact per-token KV-cache byte footprint of your target model at FP16 vs. FP8?
How does enabling prefix caching (sharing KV blocks across common system prompts) affect TTFT under load?
What happens to tail latency when a long-prompt prefill shares the same GPU batch as active decode requests (chunked prefill vs. disaggregated prefill/decode)?
How does your streaming gateway detect client SSE disconnects and abort GPU decode iterations immediately?

learningJourney.title: LLM Inference Optimization, Quantization & Continuous Batching
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate GPU idle bubbles and memory-bandwidth bottlenecks using quantization, continuous batching, and speculative decoding.

explanation.foundation: Serving LLMs at scale is a scheduling and memory-bandwidth problem.
explanation.core: Static batching forces short requests to wait until the longest sequence in the batch finishes generating EOS, wasting up to 65% of GPU cycles. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules at token-step granularity: as soon as one request emits EOS, a waiting request enters the batch on the very next forward pass.
explanation.deepDive: To prevent long prompt prefills from stalling active decode steps (ITL spikes), engines like vLLM and Sarathi-Serve use chunked prefill, slicing 8K-token prompts into 512-token chunks interleaved with decode tokens. On the weight side, FP8 and INT4 AWQ/GPTQ quantization cut HBM reads by 2x-4x for memory-bound decode, while speculative decoding uses a small draft model (or Medusa/EAGLE heads) to propose gamma=4..6 tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel forward pass without altering the output distribution.

ideas.title: Continuous Batching & Chunked Prefill
ideas.description: Iteration-level scheduling frees KV-cache slots immediately on EOS, while chunked prefill caps prompt compute per step so Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) does not stall Inter-Token Latency (ITL).

ideas.title: Speculative Decoding & Disaggregated Serving
ideas.description: Drafting K tokens cheaply and verifying them in a single target pass converts memory-bound decode into compute-bound parallel verification; disaggregated pools separate prefill GPUs from decode GPUs.

example.title: Fixing p99 ITL jitter under mixed 100-token and 12K-token prompts
example.scenario: A shared 70B inference cluster hit 950 ms p99 inter-token latency spikes whenever users submitted 12K-token RAG prompts alongside short chat turns.
example.reasoning: Each 12K-token prefill monopolized the GPU for ~850 ms, stalling all in-flight decode streams. Enabling chunked prefill (max 512 prefill tokens per iteration) and moving weights to FP8 cut p99 ITL to 42 ms while sustaining 2.1x higher request throughput.
example.lesson: Never mix unchunked long prefills with latency-sensitive decode steps; bound prefill chunk size or disaggregate prefill and decode pools.

How does speculative decoding guarantee lossless output equivalence to the target model?
When should you split prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools (disaggregated serving) instead of colocation?
Why does AWQ preserve the top 1% salient weight channels in FP16 while quantizing the remaining 99% to INT4?

learningJourney.title: Fine-Tuning, LoRA/QLoRA & Alignment (SFT, DPO, RLHF)
learningJourney.purpose: Choose rigorously between prompting, RAG, LoRA, and full fine-tuning, and align model behavior with SFT and preference optimization.

explanation.foundation: Full-parameter fine-tuning of a 70B model in FP16 with AdamW requires ~1.12 TB of VRAM (16 bytes per parameter across weights, gradients, FP32 master weights, and m/v optimizer moments).
explanation.core: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes the base weights W and injects trainable rank-r decompositions deltaW = (alpha / r) * B * A into attention and MLP projections, shrinking trainable parameters by >99% (often <0.5% of W). QLoRA pushes this further by storing frozen W in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) with double quantization and paged CPU-offloaded optimizer states, letting a 70B adapter train on a single 48-80 GB GPU.
explanation.deepDive: In production, multi-tenant LoRA serving (S-LoRA / Punica) keeps one shared base model in HBM and batches heterogeneous customer adapters in one kernel. For behavior shaping, teams run Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for format and domain style, followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) or PPO/GRPO to suppress refusals, verbosity, and policy violations.

ideas.title: RAG vs. Fine-Tuning Boundary
ideas.description: Use RAG for mutable facts, citations, and tenant ACLs; use LoRA fine-tuning for output schema adherence, specialized syntax, tone, or latency reduction via distilling a 70B teacher into an 8B student.

ideas.title: Multi-Tenant LoRA Serving (S-LoRA)
ideas.description: Instead of deploying N separate model replicas, hold one quantized base model in VRAM and execute Segmented Gather Matrix-Vector Multiplication (SGMV) across per-tenant LoRA adapters.

example.title: Distilling a 70B SQL agent into a fine-tuned 8B LoRA model
example.scenario: A SaaS analytics copilot spent $42K/month running 70B prompts with 18 few-shot examples to emit valid dialect-specific SQL at 1.4s TTFT.
example.reasoning: The team logged 50K verified 70B SQL traces, trained an r=32 QLoRA adapter on an 8B model via SFT + DPO on syntax errors, and served it behind a single FP8 base replica. Accuracy matched the 70B baseline (94.2% vs. 94.6%) while cutting TTFT to 110 ms and GPU cost by 86%.
example.lesson: Fine-tuning excels at compressing bulky few-shot instructions and teaching strict output structure, not memorizing volatile facts.

Why is injecting knowledge via fine-tuning alone risky for enterprise data with per-document ACLs?
How does DPO eliminate the separate reward model and online rollout instability of PPO-based RLHF?
How do rank r and alpha affect LoRA capacity, overfitting, and adapter memory footprint?

learningJourney.title: Agentic Workflows, Tool Calling, LangGraph & MCP
learningJourney.purpose: Architect bounded, resumable AI agents with typed tool contracts, durable checkpoints, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) safety gates.

explanation.foundation: Production agents fail when treated as unbounded 'while not done' ReAct loops.
explanation.core: Reliable systems model agent execution as a deterministic directed state graph (e.g., LangGraph) with typed state transitions, hard step/token budgets, and cycle detection. Every external action uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or strict JSON-schema tool contracts with idempotency keys so retries after network timeouts never double-charge or duplicate tickets.
explanation.deepDive: For high-blast-radius mutations (refunds, production deploys, SQL writes), the state graph persists a durable checkpoint to Postgres/Redis and emits an interrupt for Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approval before resuming. In multi-agent topologies, a Supervisor node routes scoped sub-tasks to specialized worker agents with isolated context windows so tool outputs from one domain do not pollute the global prompt.

ideas.title: Bounded State Graphs & Durable Checkpointing
ideas.description: Persist state after every node transition (plan -> tool -> observe) so long-running workflows survive worker crashes and pause cleanly for human approval.

ideas.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP) & Context Isolation
ideas.description: Decouple agent runtimes from tool integrations via standardized MCP servers, and isolate noisy raw tool payloads inside worker sub-graphs.

example.title: Stopping an infinite tool-retry loop in a customer support agent
example.scenario: An autonomous support agent burned $180 in 4 minutes on a single ticket by repeatedly calling `lookup_order` with malformed dates and retrying on 400 errors.
example.reasoning: The loop lacked a per-tool retry cap, structured error feedback, and a max-step budget. Migrating to a state graph with max_steps=8, schema-validated tool arguments, and automatic escalation to a HITL queue after 2 consecutive tool failures eliminated runaway spend.
example.lesson: Treat LLM agents as distributed workflows: enforce step budgets, idempotency keys, circuit breakers, and durable HITL checkpoints.

learningJourney.title: LLM Evaluation Harnesses, Semantic Caching & Prompt Security
learningJourney.purpose: Gate deployments with automated grounding metrics, cut repeat inference cost safely with semantic caching, and defend against prompt injection.

explanation.foundation: Because LLM outputs are non-deterministic, vibe-checking five prompts before shipping guarantees silent regressions.
explanation.core: Production teams run CI/CD evaluation harnesses (e.g., RAGAS) over golden datasets to track Context Recall, Context Precision, Faithfulness (claim-by-claim NLI against retrieved chunks), and Answer Relevance. When using LLM-as-a-Judge, mitigate position bias (swapping A/B order), verbosity bias, and self-preference using calibrated rubrics.
explanation.deepDive: On the serving path, semantic caching embeds incoming queries and checks a Redis/Qdrant cache; only high-similarity hits (cosine >= 0.94) scoped by tenant_id, ACL group, and prompt template version may short-circuit generation. Finally, defense-in-depth against direct and indirect prompt injection separates trusted system instructions from untrusted retrieved text, validates structured outputs against strict schemas, and blocks PII or secret exfiltration before responses stream to clients.

ideas.title: Decomposed RAG Evals (Retrieval vs. Generation)
ideas.description: Measure retrieval (Context Recall/Precision) separately from generation (Faithfulness/Groundedness) so you know immediately whether a failure is an indexing bug or an LLM hallucination.

ideas.title: Tenant-Scoped Semantic Caching
ideas.description: Never cache solely by raw query embedding: partition cache keys by tenant_id, ACL role, and model version, and require cosine >= 0.94 to avoid serving wrong-intent answers.

example.title: Preventing cross-tenant leaks and false hits in a semantic cache
example.scenario: A helpdesk bot enabled a global semantic cache at cosine threshold 0.85, cutting LLM spend 40%—but started returning 'How to reset Admin MFA' answers to 'How to reset Billing Card' queries and leaked internal HR policy snippets.
example.reasoning: 0.85 cosine similarity conflated structurally similar questions with different nouns, and a global cache bypassed tenant ACL filters. Tightening the threshold to 0.95, requiring exact entity-noun match on product SKUs, and keying the cache by (tenant_id, role_hash) eliminated false hits while still capturing 24% repeat FAQ traffic.
example.lesson: Semantic caches must be ACL-partitioned and conservatively thresholded (>= 0.94); false positives erode user trust faster than cache misses.

learningJourney.title: Classical ML Systems, Feature Stores & Pipeline Orchestration
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate training-serving skew and temporal data leakage with dual-engine feature stores, reproducible DAGs, and drift-aware rollouts.

explanation.foundation: Most production ranking, fraud, and recommendation systems still rely on tabular gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) or two-tower neural rankers backed by disciplined feature engineering.
explanation.core: The #1 failure mode is training-serving skew: computing a feature differently in offline Python/Spark notebooks than in the online Java/Go microservice, or leaking future labels via naive SQL joins. A Feature Store (Feast, Tecton) solves both by compiling one declarative feature definition into an offline columnar store (Parquet/BigQuery with AS-OF point-in-time joins) for training and a low-latency online KV store (Redis/DynamoDB at <10 ms p99) for inference.
explanation.deepDive: Orchestrators (Airflow, Dagster, Kubeflow) version datasets, feature snapshots, and model artifacts together, while deployment gates use shadow traffic, canary percentages, and Population Stability Index (PSI) / concept-drift monitors to catch silent accuracy decay.

ideas.title: Point-in-Time (AS-OF) Joins
ideas.description: Training datasets must join each historical label event with only the feature values that existed strictly before the event timestamp, preventing future data leakage.

ideas.title: Offline-Online Parity & Drift Monitoring
ideas.description: Share transformation code across batch backfills and streaming Flink/Kafka jobs, and monitor input feature shift (data drift) separately from label-relationship shift (concept drift).

example.title: Fixing a fraud model that scored 0.96 AUC offline and 0.61 online
example.scenario: A payment fraud classifier passed offline validation at 0.96 ROC-AUC, yet missed 35% of live fraud rings in its first week of shadow deployment.
example.reasoning: The offline training query joined `user_chargeback_count_30d` using current table state rather than an AS-OF timestamp join—leaking future chargebacks into historical training rows—while the online path defaulted missing Redis keys to 0 instead of -1.
example.lesson: Always enforce point-in-time joins in the offline store and log live online feature vectors directly for training parity.

endToEndExample.title: Production Enterprise RAG & Streaming Inference Platform
endToEndExample.scenario: An enterprise knowledge assistant serves 10M technical documents and source-code wikis to 50,000 employees, requiring sub-20ms hybrid retrieval, strict tenant ACL enforcement, grounded citations, and streaming LLM responses.

architectureFlow.name: API Gateway & Guardrail Ingress
architectureFlow.responsibility: Authenticates JWT/ACL claims, checks semantic cache (cosine >= 0.96), and screens prompts for injection.

architectureFlow.name: Query Router & Hybrid Retriever
architectureFlow.responsibility: Decomposes multi-hop queries and runs parallel Qdrant int8 HNSW + BM25 searches with ACL bitmap pre-filtering, fused via RRF.

architectureFlow.name: Cross-Encoder Reranker & Context Assembler
architectureFlow.responsibility: Reranks top-50 child chunks with BGE-reranker, expands to parent sections, and places top evidence at prompt edges.

architectureFlow.name: vLLM Serving Pool & SSE Streamer
architectureFlow.responsibility: Executes continuous-batched GQA inference with PagedAttention and prefix caching, aborting generation on SSE disconnect.

reasoning: Pre-normalized 1536-d embeddings with int8 scalar quantization and 4x FP16 rescoring keep 10M vectors in a single 64 GB RAM tier at 98% recall@10.
Parallel dense HNSW + sparse BM25 fused via RRF (k = 60) ensures exact ticket IDs and error codes rank alongside conceptual matches.
Parent-child chunking plus cross-encoder reranking bounds prompt size to ~3,000 high-signal tokens, keeping TTFT under 350ms.
Prefix caching reuses KV-cache blocks for the 800-token system prompt across all concurrent requests.
Pydantic schema validation and automated citation verification reject ungrounded claims before final UI rendering.

ACL filtering must happen inside the retrieval index, never as a post-filter.
PagedAttention, prefix caching, and disconnect-aware SSE cancellation directly control GPU unit economics.

failureScenario.recovery: Enforce strict max_input_tokens and max_output_tokens admission caps, enable chunked prefill so long prompts do not starve decode tokens, and shed excess load at the API queue with HTTP 429 + Retry-After.

knowledgeCheck.question: Your RAG pipeline uses pure dense vector search and fails whenever users search for exact error codes like 'ORA-00942' or invoice IDs like 'INV-88412'. What is the strongest architectural fix?

options.text: Increase top-k from 5 to 50 and let the LLM scan all 50 chunks.
options.feedback: If the dense bi-encoder never retrieved the exact-match chunk in the top 50, larger k still misses it—and stuffing 50 chunks worsens Lost-in-the-Middle decay and TTFT.

options.text: Run dense ANN and sparse BM25 lexical search in parallel, fuse with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and rerank the top candidates.
options.feedback: Correct. BM25 captures exact alphanumeric tokens while dense vectors capture semantics; RRF merges both rank lists without fragile score calibration.

options.text: Fine-tune the generator LLM on all invoices and error logs so it memorizes them.
options.feedback: Fine-tuning cannot reliably memorize millions of dynamic IDs or maintain real-time data freshness; retrieval is the right layer to fix.

exercises.title: Compare Full Fine-Tuning vs. QLoRA VRAM
exercises.prompt: Estimate the GPU VRAM needed for full AdamW mixed-precision fine-tuning vs. 4-bit QLoRA (rank r=16, 0.3% trainable params) on a 70B-parameter model.
reviewQuestions: Why does standard full-parameter fine-tuning require ~16 bytes of memory per model parameter with AdamW?
How does NF4 double quantization allow a 70B parameter model to fit onto a single 80 GB GPU?
What trade-off is accepted when fine-tuning only 0.3% of parameters via low-rank adapters?
steps: Full FP16 + AdamW consumes ~16 bytes/param (2B weights + 2B grads + 4B FP32 master + 8B m/v states) = 70B * 16 B = ~1,120 GB (~14x 80GB H100s before activations).
QLoRA NF4 base weights = 70B * 0.5 B = 35 GB (+ ~1.5 GB double-quant metadata).
Trainable LoRA params = 0.003 * 70B = 210M params * 16 B = ~3.36 GB; total base + optimizer fits comfortably on a single 80 GB A100/H100 (leaving ~40 GB for activations).
exercises.takeaway: QLoRA reduces weight + optimizer memory by >25x, turning a multi-node 14-GPU training job into a single-GPU workflow.

exercises.title: Size Disaggregated Prefill vs. Decode Capacity
exercises.prompt: You serve 40 req/s with average 2,000 input tokens and 250 output tokens. Compare static batching vs. continuous batching + FP8 quantization.
reviewQuestions: Why does static batching waste up to 75% of compute slots on variable-length LLM generation?
How does iteration-level continuous batching schedule new prefills alongside active token decode steps?
Why is disaggregating prefill GPUs from decode GPUs advantageous under heavy prompt loads?
steps: Total throughput demand = 40 * 2,000 = 80,000 prefill tok/s and 40 * 250 = 10,000 decode tok/s.
With static batching (max output 1,000 tokens, avg 250), 75% of decode slots sit padded/idle after short sequences finish EOS.
Switching to continuous batching eliminates slot padding (4x higher effective batch density), and FP8 halves weight HBM reads per decode step—cutting required decode GPUs by ~4-6x.
exercises.takeaway: Always size prefill (compute-bound tok/s) and decode (HBM-bandwidth-bound tok/s) separately when provisioning LLM clusters.

knowledgeChecks.question: What is the main benefit—and corresponding operational trade-off—of using Cosine Similarity in AI & Machine Learning Systems?

options.text: Advantage: Preserves both magnitude and directional separation. It has zero operational or latency overhead compared to Euclidean (L2) Distance.
options.feedback: Not quite: that describes Euclidean (L2) Distance, whereas Cosine Similarity specifically trades off: Ignores document length or popularity signals if magnitude encodes importance.

options.text: Using Dot Product (MIPS) eliminates all latency and consistency trade-offs
options.feedback: Incorrect: every production option in AI & Machine Learning Systems carries concrete latency, consistency, or operational costs.

options.text: Advantage: Invariant to vector magnitude; focuses purely on semantic direction. Cost: Ignores document length or popularity signals if magnitude encodes importance.
options.feedback: Correct: Cosine Similarity delivers invariant to vector magnitude; focuses purely on semantic direction. while requiring you to manage ignores document length or popularity signals if magnitude encodes importance.

options.text: Models trained with MRL pack coarse semantics into early dimensions, allowing a 3072-d vector to be truncated to 512-d or 256-d for fast first-stage retrieval before…

options.text: It only applies during local unit testing and can be disabled in production to save memory.

knowledgeChecks.question: A 70B LLM serving cluster suffers 900 ms inter-token latency (ITL) spikes whenever a user submits an 8K-token RAG prompt. What is the most targeted serving fix?

options.text: Increase max static batch size from 16 to 64 so more requests wait together.
options.feedback: Static batching worsens tail latency because short requests wait for the longest sequence and 8K prefills still block decode steps.

options.text: Enable continuous batching with chunked prefill (e.g., 512 tokens per step) or disaggregate prefill and decode pools.
options.feedback: Correct. Chunked prefill bounds compute per iteration so active decode streams maintain smooth ITL, while disaggregated pools isolate prefill spikes completely.

options.text: Switch model weights from BF16 to FP32 for higher numerical precision.
options.feedback: FP32 doubles HBM bandwidth per decode step and cuts GPU capacity in half, making latency worse.

knowledgeChecks.question: You want an 8B model to emit strict proprietary JSON schemas reliably at low latency, while also answering questions about daily-changing internal HR policies. What architecture fits best?

options.text: Fine-tune the 8B model nightly on all HR policy documents and skip RAG.
options.feedback: Nightly fine-tuning cannot enforce per-user document ACLs, lags behind same-day edits, and risks hallucinating outdated policy numbers.

options.text: Use QLoRA/LoRA fine-tuning (or constrained decoding) for strict JSON syntax + RAG with ACL pre-filtering for live HR policies.
options.feedback: Correct. Fine-tuning teaches stable output structure and style, while RAG supplies fresh, access-controlled, citable facts.

options.text: Disable retrieval and rely on a global semantic cache across all employees.
options.feedback: A global semantic cache without tenant/role partitioning leaks restricted HR policies across employees.

knowledgeChecks.question: An offline fraud classifier achieved 0.96 ROC-AUC in backtesting but dropped to 0.61 online. Logs show training queried current user chargeback tables directly. What caused the gap?

options.text: Temporal data leakage from missing AS-OF point-in-time joins, creating training-serving skew.
options.feedback: Correct. Joining current aggregate tables leaked future chargebacks into historical training rows; an AS-OF feature store join restricts features to timestamps strictly before each transaction.

options.text: Using XGBoost instead of a Transformer for tabular fraud features.
options.feedback: Tree ensembles routinely excel on tabular data; the 0.35 AUC cliff points to data leakage and offline-online skew, not model family.

options.text: Missing BM25 lexical fusion in the feature store.
options.feedback: BM25 applies to text retrieval, not tabular point-in-time feature joins.

learningJourney.title: Vector Embeddings, Mathematical Spaces & Similarity
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how unstructured data maps to continuous vector spaces and how distance metrics behave on hardware.
learningJourney.explanation: Embedding models project text, images, or code into dense floating-point vectors in R^D (commonly D = 768 to 3072). Choosing between Cosine similarity, Euclidean (L2) distance, and Inner Product depends on whether vector magnitude carries signal.

ideas.title: Unit Normalization at Ingest
ideas.description: Normalize embeddings to unit L2 norm once during ingestion so query-time cosine similarity executes as a pure SIMD dot product without square-root or division instructions.

ideas.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)
ideas.description: Models trained with MRL pack coarse semantics into early dimensions, allowing a 3072-d vector to be truncated to 512-d or 256-d for fast first-stage retrieval before full-dimension rescoring.

example.title: Pre-normalizing 1536-d embeddings for AVX-512 throughput
example.scenario: A semantic product-matching service ran cosine similarity across 200,000 candidate vectors per shard and hit CPU saturation during peak traffic.
example.reasoning: Profiling showed 32% of query CPU cycles went to computing vector norms on the fly. Pre-normalizing vectors at write time and switching the index metric to inner product enabled contiguous AVX-512 FMA dot products, cutting p95 scoring CPU time by 35% with identical top-k rankings.
example.lesson: Pre-normalize unit vectors at ingestion so query-time similarity becomes pure SIMD multiply-add.

reflectionQuestions: Does your embedding model produce unit-normalized vectors, or does vector magnitude carry domain signal?
Can you truncate Matryoshka dimensions (e.g., 1536 -> 512) for first-stage recall without dropping NDCG@10 below SLA?

learningJourney.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) & Vector Indexing
learningJourney.purpose: Trade bounded recall loss for sub-10ms latency and predictable RAM budgets at million-to-billion vector scale.
learningJourney.explanation: Exact K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) scans every vector in O(N * D) time, saturating DRAM bandwidth long before compute. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes eliminate exhaustive scans. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph where upper sparse layers act as express highways and lower dense layers refine the local neighborhood in O(log N) hops, tuned via M (edges per node), efConstruction, and efSearch.

ideas.title: Two-Stage Oversampling and Rescoring
ideas.description: Retrieve top 4*K candidates using compressed int8 or PQ codes in RAM, then fetch full-precision FP32/FP16 vectors from NVMe or RAM to compute exact distances for the final top K.

ideas.title: Segment-Based Immutable Indexing
ideas.description: Buffer live vector writes in a WAL and small mutable segment while merging immutable HNSW segments asynchronously in the background so compaction never stalls query threads.

example.title: Fitting 50M 1536-d vectors into a 64 GB RAM node
example.scenario: Storing 50M 1536-d FP32 vectors in an unquantized HNSW graph required ~360 GB of RAM, forcing an expensive 6-node memory-optimized cluster.
example.reasoning: Switched to Scalar Quantization (int8) with HNSW oversampling (4x) and exact FP16 rescoring from NVMe. RAM dropped by 74% to ~52 GB on a single node while keeping recall@10 at 98.1% and p99 latency at 11ms.
example.lesson: Quantize in-memory index vectors and oversample + rescore exact vectors from fast storage.

reflectionQuestions: What is the total RAM footprint of raw vectors plus HNSW graph edges (M * 2 * 4 bytes/node) at your 12-month target scale?
How does selectivity of metadata filters affect HNSW graph connectivity during pre-filtering vs. post-filtering?

example.reasoning: Deployed parallel Qdrant HNSW dense retrieval and BM25 inverted-index search, merging top-100 candidates from each leg via RRF (k = 60). Exact identifier recall hit 99.4% and overall NDCG@10 improved by 42% at 18ms p95 latency.
example.lesson: Pair dense embeddings with sparse lexical retrieval via RRF whenever queries include exact identifiers or domain jargon.

learningJourney.title: Vector Embeddings, Mathematical Spaces & Similarity
learningJourney.purpose: Understand how unstructured data maps to continuous vector spaces and how distance metrics behave on hardware.
learningJourney.explanation: Embedding models project text, images, or code into dense floating-point vectors in R^D (commonly D = 768 to 3072). Choosing between Cosine similarity, Euclidean (L2) distance, and Inner Product depends on whether vector magnitude carries signal. When vectors are L2-normalized to unit length (||v|| = 1), Euclidean squared distance reduces to 2 - 2(a · b), making Cosine, L2, and Dot Product rank-equivalent while letting CPUs compute similarity as raw AVX-512 or NEON SIMD dot products. In high dimensions, random vector distances concentrate around their mean (curse of dimensionality), so models trained with contrastive or Matryoshka losses are required to preserve meaningful angular separation.

ideas.title: Unit Normalization at Ingest
ideas.description: Normalize embeddings to unit L2 norm once during ingestion so query-time cosine similarity executes as a pure SIMD dot product without square-root or division instructions.

ideas.title: Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL)
ideas.description: Models trained with MRL pack coarse semantics into early dimensions, allowing a 3072-d vector to be truncated to 512-d or 256-d for fast first-stage retrieval before full-dimension rescoring.

example.title: Pre-normalizing 1536-d embeddings for AVX-512 throughput
example.scenario: A semantic product-matching service ran cosine similarity across 200,000 candidate vectors per shard and hit CPU saturation during peak traffic.
example.reasoning: Profiling showed 32% of query CPU cycles went to computing vector norms on the fly. Pre-normalizing vectors at write time and switching the index metric to inner product enabled contiguous AVX-512 FMA dot products, cutting p95 scoring CPU time by 35% with identical top-k rankings.
example.lesson: Pre-normalize unit vectors at ingestion so query-time similarity becomes pure SIMD multiply-add.

reflectionQuestions: Does your embedding model produce unit-normalized vectors, or does vector magnitude carry domain signal?
Can you truncate Matryoshka dimensions (e.g., 1536 -> 512) for first-stage recall without dropping NDCG@10 below SLA?
How will you handle re-indexing when upgrading to a new embedding model whose vector space is incompatible?

learningJourney.title: Approximate Nearest Neighbors (ANN) & Vector Indexing
learningJourney.purpose: Trade bounded recall loss for sub-10ms latency and predictable RAM budgets at million-to-billion vector scale.
learningJourney.explanation: Exact K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) scans every vector in O(N * D) time, saturating DRAM bandwidth long before compute. Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexes eliminate exhaustive scans. HNSW builds a multi-layer proximity graph where upper sparse layers act as express highways and lower dense layers refine the local neighborhood in O(log N) hops, tuned via M (edges per node), efConstruction, and efSearch. Inverted File (IVF) indexes partition the space into k Voronoi cells via k-means and scan only the nearest nprobe cells. To fit billion-scale corpora in RAM, Product Quantization (PQ) splits a D-dimensional vector into M sub-vectors and encodes each to an 8-bit centroid ID—compressing a 1536-d FP32 vector (6,144 bytes) down to 96 bytes (64x compression) at the cost of slight quantization error.

ideas.title: Two-Stage Oversampling and Rescoring
ideas.description: Retrieve top 4*K candidates using compressed int8 or PQ codes in RAM, then fetch full-precision FP32/FP16 vectors from NVMe or RAM to compute exact distances for the final top K.

ideas.title: Segment-Based Immutable Indexing
ideas.description: Buffer live vector writes in a WAL and small mutable segment while merging immutable HNSW segments asynchronously in the background so compaction never stalls query threads.

example.title: Fitting 50M 1536-d vectors into a 64 GB RAM node
example.scenario: Storing 50M 1536-d FP32 vectors in an unquantized HNSW graph required ~360 GB of RAM, forcing an expensive 6-node memory-optimized cluster.
example.reasoning: Switched to Scalar Quantization (int8) with HNSW oversampling (4x) and exact FP16 rescoring from NVMe. RAM dropped by 74% to ~52 GB on a single node while keeping recall@10 at 98.1% and p99 latency at 11ms.
example.lesson: Quantize in-memory index vectors and oversample + rescore exact vectors from fast storage.

reflectionQuestions: What is the total RAM footprint of raw vectors plus HNSW graph edges (M * 2 * 4 bytes/node) at your 12-month target scale?
How does selectivity of metadata filters affect HNSW graph connectivity during pre-filtering vs. post-filtering?

learningJourney.title: Hybrid Search: Dense Semantic Vectors & Sparse BM25
learningJourney.purpose: Combine conceptual semantic recall with exact lexical precision using calibrated rank fusion.
learningJourney.explanation: Dense bi-encoder embeddings compress entire passages into a single fixed-width vector, which blurs rare tokens, exact SKUs, stack traces, and invoice IDs. Sparse lexical algorithms like BM25 score exact term matches using saturated term frequency (k1) and document-length normalization (b) weighted by Inverse Document Frequency (IDF), while neural sparse models like SPLADE expand documents into learned vocabulary weights. Because BM25 scores are unbounded positive floats and cosine scores lie in [-1, 1], summing raw scores directly is unstable. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) merges ranked lists purely by position: RRF(d) = sum(1 / (k + rank_i(d))) with k = 60, ensuring documents ranked highly by both retrievers rise deterministically.

ideas.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)
ideas.description: Fuse dense and sparse rankings using 1 / (60 + rank) so neither retriever's raw score scale dominates without fragile min-max calibration.

ideas.title: SPLADE Learned Sparse Expansion
ideas.description: Use a masked-language-model head to project passages into high-dimensional sparse vectors that capture synonyms (e.g. 'car' -> 'automobile') while remaining compatible with inverted indexes.

example.title: Sub-20ms hybrid semantic search at 10M document scale
example.scenario: An enterprise document platform using pure dense embeddings failed when finance teams searched exact invoice IDs like 'INV-90210' or error codes like 'ERR_QUOTA_429', returning topically similar but wrong memos.
example.reasoning: Deployed parallel Qdrant HNSW dense retrieval and BM25 inverted-index search, merging top-100 candidates from each leg via RRF (k = 60). Exact identifier recall hit 99.4% and overall NDCG@10 improved by 42% at 18ms p95 latency.
example.lesson: Pair dense embeddings with sparse lexical retrieval via RRF whenever queries include exact identifiers or domain jargon.

reflectionQuestions: Which query classes in your workload require exact token matching (IDs, error codes, proper nouns) vs. semantic paraphrasing?
Should dense and sparse legs carry equal weight in RRF, or do domain benchmarks justify weighted rank fusion?
How do you tokenize compound technical identifiers (camelCase, snake_case, hyphenated SKUs) in your BM25 analyzer?

learningJourney.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Architecture
learningJourney.purpose: Design multi-stage retrieval pipelines that ground LLM generation in fresh, access-controlled data.
learningJourney.explanation: Naive RAG—embed a raw user query, fetch top-k chunks, and stuff them into a prompt—fails on ambiguous phrasing, multi-hop questions, and strict ACL filtering. Short user questions occupy a different region of embedding space than long declarative answers; HyDE bridges this gap by generating a hypothetical answer first and embedding that passage. Multi-query expansion and sub-query decomposition split compound requests into parallel retrievals. Equally critical is enforcing tenant and document permissions via metadata pre-filtering inside the index rather than post-filtering, which can return zero results when an authorized subset is small.

ideas.title: HyDE Alignment
ideas.description: Generate a brief hypothetical answer using a fast small model and embed it to match declarative document passages more closely than a raw question.

ideas.title: ACL Pre-Filtering
ideas.description: Evaluate tenant and role predicates during graph traversal or via bitmap filters so unauthorized chunks never consume top-k slots.

example.title: Decomposing multi-hop financial compliance queries
example.scenario: Analysts asking 'How did EMEA Q2 churn compare against Q1 policy changes?' received incomplete answers because single-vector search only matched Q2 earnings chunks.
example.reasoning: Added an LLM query decomposer that split the prompt into two parallel sub-queries scoped by quarter metadata filters ('Q1 policy' and 'Q2 EMEA churn'), then merged results before synthesis. Answer faithfulness on the eval suite rose from 61% to 93%.
example.lesson: Complex questions require query decomposition and metadata-scoped retrieval, not a larger top-k.

learningJourney.title: Chunking Strategies, Context Compression & Reranking
learningJourney.purpose: Maximize signal-to-noise ratio in the LLM context window through smart chunking and cross-encoder reranking.
learningJourney.explanation: Bi-encoder embeddings encode queries and documents independently in O(1) vector lookups, losing fine-grained token-to-token interactions. Cross-encoders concatenate (query, chunk) and run full self-attention across both, producing dramatically more accurate relevance scores at O((L_q + L_d)^2) compute cost—making them ideal as a second-stage filter over the top 50–100 hybrid hits. Chunking faces a core tension: small chunks (128–256 tokens) yield sharp embeddings, while LLMs need surrounding context (1024+ tokens) to reason accurately. Parent-child indexing resolves this by indexing small child chunks while returning their parent section to the generator, and placing the highest-ranked chunks at the start and end of the prompt mitigates the 'Lost in the Middle' attention decay.
caveats: Cross-encoder latency scales linearly with candidate count K; cap reranking to top 30-50 chunks or run on dedicated GPU batching.
Fixed-character chunking splits tables, code blocks, and sentences mid-thought; use structure-aware or recursive splitters.
Stuffing 30+ chunks into long-context windows inflates TTFT (Time to First Token) quadratically during prefill and degrades accuracy.

ideas.title: Parent-Child Retrieval
ideas.description: Embed 150-token child windows for high retrieval precision, then map hits back to their 1,000-token parent block for coherent LLM synthesis.

ideas.title: Edge-Weighted Context Ordering
ideas.description: Place the top-1 and top-2 reranked passages at the beginning and end of the prompt context to counter U-shaped transformer attention decay.

example.title: Eliminating missed clauses in 100-page legal contract QA
example.scenario: A legal assistant injected top-30 500-token chunks into the prompt, yet the LLM repeatedly missed exception clauses placed in chunks 12 through 22.
example.reasoning: Switched to clause-aware parent-child indexing (200-token child chunks linked to full section parents) and added a BGE-reranker-v2 cross-encoder to prune top-50 hits down to the top 5 ordered at prompt edges. Hallucinated or missed exceptions dropped by 68% and prefill latency fell 45%.
example.lesson: Rerank aggressively to a small, high-signal context rather than relying on raw context-window size.

Is a 40-80ms cross-encoder rerank step justified by the resulting drop in downstream LLM token cost and hallucinations?

learningJourney.title: Deep Learning Foundations & GPU Tensor Hardware
learningJourney.purpose: Understand tensor memory layouts, autograd graphs, Tensor Cores, and the GPU Roofline model.
learningJourney.explanation: Deep learning workloads are governed by GPU hardware physics. Tensors are N-dimensional views over contiguous 1D memory buffers indexed via shape and stride metadata; non-contiguous transposes must be materialized before coalesced GPU memory reads. Training builds a dynamic or static computation graph for reverse-mode automatic differentiation (autograd), storing intermediate activations in VRAM unless activation checkpointing recomputes them on the fly. On modern GPUs, Tensor Cores execute warp-level Matrix Multiply-Accumulate (MMA) in FP16, BF16, or FP8 at hundreds of teraflops. By the Roofline model, arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved from HBM) determines whether an operation is compute-bound (LLM prompt prefill, large GEMMs) or memory-bandwidth-bound (token-by-token LLM decode, elementwise activations).

ideas.title: Prefill vs. Decode Roofline Split
ideas.description: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel as large matrix-matrix multiplications (compute-bound), whereas autoregressive decode processes 1 token per sequence per step (HBM bandwidth-bound).

ideas.title: BF16 & FP8 Precision Trade-offs
ideas.description: BF16 preserves FP32's 8-bit exponent range to prevent training gradient underflow, while FP8 cuts weight and KV-cache HBM traffic in half during inference.

example.title: Breaking the HBM bandwidth wall in 70B decode
example.scenario: A 70B FP16 model on 2x H100 GPUs showed only 8% Tensor Core compute utilization during decode despite 100% HBM bandwidth saturation.
example.reasoning: Each decode step streamed ~140 GB of weights from HBM for a single token per request. Quantizing weights to FP8 (halving HBM bytes per token) and enabling continuous batching raised arithmetic intensity across concurrent sequences, boosting decode tokens/sec by 2.4x.
example.lesson: Autoregressive LLM decode is gated by HBM memory bandwidth; increase batching or quantize weights to raise arithmetic intensity.

reflectionQuestions: Which phase of your inference pipeline is compute-bound (TTFT/prefill) vs. HBM bandwidth-bound (ITL/decode)?
When does kernel fusion (e.g., `torch.compile` / Triton) eliminate intermediate HBM round-trips for elementwise ops?
How much VRAM must be reserved for activation memory vs. model weights vs. KV-cache?
Does FP8 or INT4 AWQ quantization introduce unacceptable perplexity or tool-calling regression on your eval set?

learningJourney.title: Transformer Architecture & Attention Physics
learningJourney.purpose: Master attention math, FlashAttention SRAM tiling, GQA/MQA, RoPE, and PagedAttention KV-caching.
learningJourney.explanation: Scaled Dot-Product Attention computes Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d_k)) * V, where scaling by sqrt(d_k) keeps dot-product variance near 1 so softmax gradients do not vanish. Materializing the N x N attention matrix in HBM scales quadratically in memory and bandwidth; FlashAttention tiles Q, K, and V blocks into fast on-chip GPU SRAM and computes softmax incrementally via online rescaling, keeping memory O(N). During autoregressive generation, caching past K and V tensors avoids recomputing the prefix, but KV-cache size (2 * layers * kv_heads * d_head * bytes_per_param * seq_len) quickly dominates VRAM. Grouped-Query Attention (GQA) shares K/V heads across groups of Q heads to shrink KV-cache traffic, RoPE encodes relative token positions via 2D rotations, and PagedAttention allocates KV-cache in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks to eliminate fragmentation.

ideas.title: FlashAttention Online Softmax Tiling
ideas.description: Fuse QK^T, masking, softmax, and V multiplication inside GPU SRAM tiles so the quadratic N x N score matrix is never written to slow HBM.

ideas.title: PagedAttention Virtual KV Blocks
ideas.description: Manage KV-cache like OS virtual memory pages so sequences grow dynamically without reserving contiguous max-context VRAM buffers.

example.title: Eliminating 60% VRAM waste with PagedAttention and continuous batching
example.scenario: A customer-support AI cluster on 8x A100 GPUs suffered OOM crashes during morning traffic spikes and dropped 14% of active sessions due to static max-length KV-cache pre-allocation.
example.reasoning: Migrated serving to vLLM using PagedAttention and iteration-level continuous batching. KV-cache internal fragmentation dropped from ~60% to under 4%, quadrupling concurrent request capacity and cutting monthly GPU spend by 58%.
example.lesson: KV-cache memory management—not raw FLOPs—determines concurrent LLM serving capacity.

learningJourney.title: LLM Inference Optimization, Quantization & Continuous Batching
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate GPU idle bubbles and memory-bandwidth bottlenecks using quantization, continuous batching, and speculative decoding.
learningJourney.explanation: Serving LLMs at scale is a scheduling and memory-bandwidth problem. Static batching forces short requests to wait until the longest sequence in the batch finishes generating EOS, wasting up to 65% of GPU cycles. Continuous (iteration-level) batching schedules at token-step granularity: as soon as one request emits EOS, a waiting request enters the batch on the very next forward pass. To prevent long prompt prefills from stalling active decode steps (ITL spikes), engines like vLLM and Sarathi-Serve use chunked prefill, slicing 8K-token prompts into 512-token chunks interleaved with decode tokens. On the weight side, FP8 and INT4 AWQ/GPTQ quantization cut HBM reads by 2x-4x for memory-bound decode, while speculative decoding uses a small draft model (or Medusa/EAGLE heads) to propose gamma=4..6 tokens that the target model verifies in one parallel forward pass without altering the output distribution.

ideas.title: Continuous Batching & Chunked Prefill
ideas.description: Iteration-level scheduling frees KV-cache slots immediately on EOS, while chunked prefill caps prompt compute per step so Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) does not stall Inter-Token Latency (ITL).

ideas.title: Speculative Decoding & Disaggregated Serving
ideas.description: Drafting K tokens cheaply and verifying them in a single target pass converts memory-bound decode into compute-bound parallel verification; disaggregated pools separate prefill GPUs from decode GPUs.

example.title: Fixing p99 ITL jitter under mixed 100-token and 12K-token prompts
example.scenario: A shared 70B inference cluster hit 950 ms p99 inter-token latency spikes whenever users submitted 12K-token RAG prompts alongside short chat turns.
example.reasoning: Each 12K-token prefill monopolized the GPU for ~850 ms, stalling all in-flight decode streams. Enabling chunked prefill (max 512 prefill tokens per iteration) and moving weights to FP8 cut p99 ITL to 42 ms while sustaining 2.1x higher request throughput.
example.lesson: Never mix unchunked long prefills with latency-sensitive decode steps; bound prefill chunk size or disaggregate prefill and decode pools.

learningJourney.title: Fine-Tuning, LoRA/QLoRA & Alignment (SFT, DPO, RLHF)
learningJourney.purpose: Choose rigorously between prompting, RAG, LoRA, and full fine-tuning, and align model behavior with SFT and preference optimization.
learningJourney.explanation: Full-parameter fine-tuning of a 70B model in FP16 with AdamW requires ~1.12 TB of VRAM (16 bytes per parameter across weights, gradients, FP32 master weights, and m/v optimizer moments). Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) freezes the base weights W and injects trainable rank-r decompositions deltaW = (alpha / r) * B * A into attention and MLP projections, shrinking trainable parameters by >99% (often <0.5% of W). QLoRA pushes this further by storing frozen W in 4-bit NormalFloat (NF4) with double quantization and paged CPU-offloaded optimizer states, letting a 70B adapter train on a single 48-80 GB GPU. In production, multi-tenant LoRA serving (S-LoRA / Punica) keeps one shared base model in HBM and batches heterogeneous customer adapters in one kernel. For behavior shaping, teams run Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) for format and domain style, followed by Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) or PPO/GRPO to suppress refusals, verbosity, and policy violations.

example.title: Distilling a 70B SQL agent into a fine-tuned 8B LoRA model
example.scenario: A SaaS analytics copilot spent $42K/month running 70B prompts with 18 few-shot examples to emit valid dialect-specific SQL at 1.4s TTFT.
example.reasoning: The team logged 50K verified 70B SQL traces, trained an r=32 QLoRA adapter on an 8B model via SFT + DPO on syntax errors, and served it behind a single FP8 base replica. Accuracy matched the 70B baseline (94.2% vs. 94.6%) while cutting TTFT to 110 ms and GPU cost by 86%.
example.lesson: Fine-tuning excels at compressing bulky few-shot instructions and teaching strict output structure, not memorizing volatile facts.

learningJourney.title: Agentic Workflows, Tool Calling, LangGraph & MCP
learningJourney.purpose: Architect bounded, resumable AI agents with typed tool contracts, durable checkpoints, and Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) safety gates.
learningJourney.explanation: Production agents fail when treated as unbounded 'while not done' ReAct loops. Reliable systems model agent execution as a deterministic directed state graph (e.g., LangGraph) with typed state transitions, hard step/token budgets, and cycle detection. Every external action uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) or strict JSON-schema tool contracts with idempotency keys so retries after network timeouts never double-charge or duplicate tickets. For high-blast-radius mutations (refunds, production deploys, SQL writes), the state graph persists a durable checkpoint to Postgres/Redis and emits an interrupt for Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) approval before resuming. In multi-agent topologies, a Supervisor node routes scoped sub-tasks to specialized worker agents with isolated context windows so tool outputs from one domain do not pollute the global prompt.

ideas.description: Persist state after every node transition (plan -> tool -> observe) so long-running workflows survive worker crashes and pause cleanly for human approval.

example.title: Stopping an infinite tool-retry loop in a customer support agent
example.scenario: An autonomous support agent burned $180 in 4 minutes on a single ticket by repeatedly calling `lookup_order` with malformed dates and retrying on 400 errors.
example.reasoning: The loop lacked a per-tool retry cap, structured error feedback, and a max-step budget. Migrating to a state graph with max_steps=8, schema-validated tool arguments, and automatic escalation to a HITL queue after 2 consecutive tool failures eliminated runaway spend.
example.lesson: Treat LLM agents as distributed workflows: enforce step budgets, idempotency keys, circuit breakers, and durable HITL checkpoints.

reflectionQuestions: Why should high-risk tool calls use durable state checkpoints and HITL interrupts rather than synchronous timeouts?
How does an idempotency key prevent duplicate side effects when an agent retries a timed-out tool call?
When does a Supervisor + specialized workers topology outperform a single monolithic agent with 40 tools?
How does MCP standardize tool, resource, and prompt discovery across heterogeneous agent clients?

learningJourney.title: LLM Evaluation Harnesses, Semantic Caching & Prompt Security
learningJourney.purpose: Gate deployments with automated grounding metrics, cut repeat inference cost safely with semantic caching, and defend against prompt injection.
learningJourney.explanation: Because LLM outputs are non-deterministic, vibe-checking five prompts before shipping guarantees silent regressions. Production teams run CI/CD evaluation harnesses (e.g., RAGAS) over golden datasets to track Context Recall, Context Precision, Faithfulness (claim-by-claim NLI against retrieved chunks), and Answer Relevance. When using LLM-as-a-Judge, mitigate position bias (swapping A/B order), verbosity bias, and self-preference using calibrated rubrics. On the serving path, semantic caching embeds incoming queries and checks a Redis/Qdrant cache; only high-similarity hits (cosine >= 0.94) scoped by tenant_id, ACL group, and prompt template version may short-circuit generation. Finally, defense-in-depth against direct and indirect prompt injection separates trusted system instructions from untrusted retrieved text, validates structured outputs against strict schemas, and blocks PII or secret exfiltration before responses stream to clients.

ideas.title: Decomposed RAG Evals (Retrieval vs. Generation)
ideas.description: Measure retrieval (Context Recall/Precision) separately from generation (Faithfulness/Groundedness) so you know immediately whether a failure is an indexing bug or an LLM hallucination.

ideas.title: Tenant-Scoped Semantic Caching
ideas.description: Never cache solely by raw query embedding: partition cache keys by tenant_id, ACL role, and model version, and require cosine >= 0.94 to avoid serving wrong-intent answers.

example.title: Preventing cross-tenant leaks and false hits in a semantic cache
example.scenario: A helpdesk bot enabled a global semantic cache at cosine threshold 0.85, cutting LLM spend 40%—but started returning 'How to reset Admin MFA' answers to 'How to reset Billing Card' queries and leaked internal HR policy snippets.
example.reasoning: 0.85 cosine similarity conflated structurally similar questions with different nouns, and a global cache bypassed tenant ACL filters. Tightening the threshold to 0.95, requiring exact entity-noun match on product SKUs, and keying the cache by (tenant_id, role_hash) eliminated false hits while still capturing 24% repeat FAQ traffic.
example.lesson: Semantic caches must be ACL-partitioned and conservatively thresholded (>= 0.94); false positives erode user trust faster than cache misses.

reflectionQuestions: How do Faithfulness and Context Recall pinpoint different failure modes in a RAG pipeline?
Why must LLM-as-a-Judge pairwise evaluations randomize A/B ordering and normalize response length?
What security vulnerability arises if a semantic cache is shared across users with different document permissions?
How does indirect prompt injection work when malicious instructions are embedded inside a retrieved webpage or PDF?

learningJourney.title: Classical ML Systems, Feature Stores & Pipeline Orchestration
learningJourney.purpose: Eliminate training-serving skew and temporal data leakage with dual-engine feature stores, reproducible DAGs, and drift-aware rollouts.
learningJourney.explanation: Most production ranking, fraud, and recommendation systems still rely on tabular gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost/LightGBM) or two-tower neural rankers backed by disciplined feature engineering. The #1 failure mode is training-serving skew: computing a feature differently in offline Python/Spark notebooks than in the online Java/Go microservice, or leaking future labels via naive SQL joins. A Feature Store (Feast, Tecton) solves both by compiling one declarative feature definition into an offline columnar store (Parquet/BigQuery with AS-OF point-in-time joins) for training and a low-latency online KV store (Redis/DynamoDB at <10 ms p99) for inference. Orchestrators (Airflow, Dagster, Kubeflow) version datasets, feature snapshots, and model artifacts together, while deployment gates use shadow traffic, canary percentages, and Population Stability Index (PSI) / concept-drift monitors to catch silent accuracy decay.

ideas.title: Point-in-Time (AS-OF) Joins
ideas.description: Training datasets must join each historical label event with only the feature values that existed strictly before the event timestamp, preventing future data leakage.

ideas.title: Offline-Online Parity & Drift Monitoring
ideas.description: Share transformation code across batch backfills and streaming Flink/Kafka jobs, and monitor input feature shift (data drift) separately from label-relationship shift (concept drift).

example.title: Fixing a fraud model that scored 0.96 AUC offline and 0.61 online
example.scenario: A payment fraud classifier passed offline validation at 0.96 ROC-AUC, yet missed 35% of live fraud rings in its first week of shadow deployment.
example.reasoning: The offline training query joined `user_chargeback_count_30d` using current table state rather than an AS-OF timestamp join—leaking future chargebacks into historical training rows—while the online path defaulted missing Redis keys to 0 instead of -1.
example.lesson: Always enforce point-in-time joins in the offline store and log live online feature vectors directly for training parity.

reflectionQuestions: How does an AS-OF point-in-time join prevent temporal data leakage when building training sets?
Why do production teams log live served feature vectors instead of reconstructing them later from warehouse tables?
What is the difference between data drift (covariate shift) and concept drift, and how do you detect each?
When should a feature be computed in batch (hourly/daily) vs. streaming (sliding 5-minute window in Flink)?
